name: Ulimorelin
lead: Ulimorelin (TZP-101) is an investigational small-molecule ghrelin receptor agonist, developed by Tranzyme Pharma as a gut prokinetic.[1] Because it acts on the same receptor as the hunger hormone ghrelin, people interested in appetite and body weight discuss it as a peripherally acting ghrelin agonist. The appearance link runs through appetite, feeding tolerance and digestive function in people who want to gain or keep weight: a compound that helps food move through the gut is a different tool from one that raises growth hormone.

It is a macrocyclic peptidomimetic found by screening Tranzyme's macrocycle library against the human ghrelin receptor and then optimised for pharmacokinetics.[1][2] It was given intravenously in early trials for postoperative ileus and diabetic gastroparesis, where phase 2 results were encouraging.[3][4]

Two phase 3 trials (ULISES 007 and 008) tested daily infusions after partial bowel resection.[5] A later phase 2 trial compared it with metoclopramide in 120 critically ill patients with enteral feeding intolerance.[6] Ulimorelin has not been approved as a medicine, and it has only been studied as an intravenous drug in hospital settings.

angle.text: Ulimorelin is discussed as a ghrelin-pathway compound that increases gut motility rather than a growth hormone booster. People interested in gaining or maintaining weight follow it for its link to feeding tolerance.

infobox: Postoperative ileus, gastroparesis, enteral feeding intolerance

paras: Tranzyme's high-throughput screen against the ghrelin receptor, using a calcium-signalling assay, produced macrocyclic hits that were potent in vitro but had poor pharmacokinetic properties. Medicinal chemistry work to improve them led to ulimorelin.[2] The molecule is a macrocycle whose molecular weight and lipophilicity fall outside the usual rule-of-five limits for oral drugs, a point the discovery paper addresses as part of the optimisation.[2]
Ulimorelin carries the code name TZP-101 and has an International Nonproprietary Name; its molecular formula is C30H39FN4O4 and its molar mass about 538.7 g/mol.[18]

Ulimorelin activates the ghrelin receptor (GHSR-1a), the receptor engaged by the stomach-derived hunger hormone ghrelin, which increases gastric emptying and colonic motility.[1][18] A review of ghrelin and motilin agonists discussed whether such compounds can be made to signal through particular pathways (biased agonism) for longer-lasting prokinetic effects, citing work in which ulimorelin produced prolonged increases in rat colorectal propulsion while responses to other ghrelin agonists faded.[1] A rat study examined the mechanism behind its effect on defecation.[13]

Separate rat studies found that ulimorelin lowers blood pressure through a vascular mechanism that does not depend on the classic ghrelin receptor.[10][11] Wikipedia notes that blood-pressure effects were not seen in human trials.[18]

A phase 1 study in healthy adults examined why once-daily dosing had not worked in postoperative ileus, a condition in which the colon recovers last. Dosing every 8 hours produced sustained gastric emptying improvements of 23% to 46%, measured by scintigraphy, with colonic transit assessed in a separate part of the study.[9]

Phase 2 testing began in 2007 with a trial of 267 patients after major open abdominal surgery and a trial of 78 patients with severe diabetic gastroparesis.[7][8] In the subset of diabetic gastroparesis patients with severe nausea and vomiting, investigators reported relief of upper gastrointestinal symptoms.[4] A covariate analysis of the postoperative phase 2 data in 236 patients undergoing partial colectomy found faster gut recovery with ulimorelin than placebo, independent of opioid use and surgery type; opioid use itself lengthened recovery.[3]

In the phase 3 ULISES programme, patients received 30-minute intravenous infusions once daily after partial bowel resection, with the main outcome the time to the later of first bowel movement and tolerance of solid food.[5] Registrations list about 330 participants in each of ULISES 007 and 008.[14][15]

In the PROMOTE trial, 120 intensive care patients with enteral feeding intolerance were randomised to ulimorelin or metoclopramide for 5 days; the primary outcome was the percentage of the daily protein prescription received, and the two drugs gave comparable results.[6][12]

Ulimorelin is not marketed and no regulator has approved it. It appears mainly in pharmacology and gastroenterology literature as one of several ghrelin and motilin receptor agonists that showed early promise as prokinetics; a review of the field noted that another ghrelin agonist, TZP-102, was inactive in gastroparesis patients.[1] Interest from the appetite and weight community comes from its ghrelin-receptor mechanism.

Human studies of ulimorelin have been conducted in hospital patients and healthy volunteers, not in people seeking cosmetic or physique change. Phase 2 trials reported faster return of bowel function after partial colectomy and symptom relief in severe diabetic gastroparesis.[3][4] Two phase 3 trials of once-daily infusions after bowel resection were completed and published in 2013.[5] A phase 1 study later concluded that once-daily dosing may have missed the colon and that 8-hourly dosing sustained gastric emptying gains.[9] PROMOTE found feeding outcomes comparable to metoclopramide in ICU patients.[6]
Phase 1 registrations also cover studies in people with hepatic impairment, a drug interaction study with midazolam, and a mass-balance study of radiolabelled drug.[16][17]

timeline.event: Phase 2 trials of TZP-101 begin in postoperative ileus and diabetic gastroparesis.[7][8]
Phase 3 ULISES 007 and 008 trials start; medicinal chemistry paper published.[2][5]

card.summary: An investigational gut-acting ghrelin receptor agonist, tested to speed digestion and feeding, followed by people interested in appetite and weight.
card.note: Investigational; given by IV in trials and not approved.

quick.overview:
Ulimorelin (TZP-101) is a ghrelin receptor agonist built to speed movement through the gut. It was tested in post-surgery bowel recovery, gastroparesis and ICU feeding problems.

People interested in appetite and weight follow it as a ghrelin-pathway compound that acts mainly on digestion.
quick.mechanism: It activates the ghrelin receptor on gut nerves and muscle, which increases gastric emptying and colonic motility. Dosing frequency mattered in trials, since once-daily dosing did not sustain the effect.
quick.risks: Trials reported it as generally well tolerated, though phase 3 postoperative ileus studies did not meet expectations and it is not approved. Rat studies show a blood-pressure-lowering effect through a separate mechanism.
